title: He who has seen me has seen the Father
source_text: Ἀλλὰ καὶ λέγων ὁ Πλάτων ὅτι τὸν „εὑρόντα ἀδύνατόν“ ἐστιν „εἰς πάντας λέγειν“ „τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦ παντὸς,“ ἄῤῥητον μὲν καὶ ἀκατονόμαστον οὔ φησιν αὐτὸν εἶναι ῥητὸν δ᾿ ὄντα εἰς ὀλίγους δύνασθαι λέγεσθαι. εἶθ᾿ ὥσπερ ἐπιλαθόμενος ὧν παρέθετο Πλάτωνος λέξεων ὁ Κέλσος φησὶν ἀκατονόμαστον εἶναι θεὸν τούτοις· ἐπειδὴ δὲ τούτου χάριν ἐξηύρηται σοφοῖς ἀνδράσιν, ὡς ἂν τοῦ ἀκατονομάστου καὶ πρώτου λάβοιμέν τινα ἐπίνοιαν. ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ μόνον τὸν θεὸν ἄῤῥητον εἶναί φαμεν ἀλλὰ καὶ ἕτερα τῶν μετ᾿ αὐτόν· ἅπερ βιασάμενος ὁ Παῦλος σημῆναί φησι τό· „ἤκουσεν ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι,“ τῷ „ἤκουσεν“ ἀντὶ τοῦ συνῆκε χρησάμενος ἀνάλογον τῷ „ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω.“ „τὸν ποιητὴν“ δὴ „καὶ πατέρα τοῦ παντὸς“ ἡμεῖς φαμεν ἰδεῖν „ἔργον.“ βλέπεται δὲ οὐ μόνον κατὰ τὸ „μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ, ὅτι αὐτοὶ τὸν θεὸν ὄψονται,“ ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὸ λεγόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς εἰκόνος „τοῦ ἀοράτου θεοῦ“ ἐν τῷ „ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα τὸν πέμψαντά με.“ ἐν τούτοις γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἂν νοῦν ἔχων φήσειεν ὅτι ἀναφέρων ταῦτα ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπὶ τὸ αἰσθητὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ βλεπόμενον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις σῶμα εἶπε τό· „ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα τὸν πέμψαντά με“· ἔσονται γὰρ κατὰ τοῦτο ἑωρακότες τὸν πατέρα θεὸν καὶ πάντες οἱ λέγοντες· „σταύρου σταύρου αὐτὸν“ καὶ ὁ ἐξουσίαν κατὰ τοῦ ἀνθρωπίνου αὐτοῦ Πιλᾶτος λαβὼν, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἄτοπον. ὅτι δὲ τὸ „ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα τὸν πέμψαντά με“ οὐκ ἐπὶ τὴν κοινοτέραν ἐκδοχὴν ἀναφέρεται, δῆλον ἐκ τοῦ εἰρῆσθαι τῷ Φιλίππῳ· „τοσούτῳ χρόνῳ μεθ᾿ ὑμῶν εἰμι, καὶ οὐκ ἔγνωκάς με, Φίλιππε;“ τοῦτο δ᾿ εἴρηκεν αὐτῷ ἀξιώσαντι καὶ λέγοντι· „δεῖξον ἡμῖν τὸν πατέρα, καὶ ἀρκεῖ ἡμῖν.“ νοήσας τις οὖν πῶς δεῖ ἀκούειν περὶ μονογενοῦς θεοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, τοῦ πρωτοτόκου „πάσης κτίσεως,“ καθότι „ὁ λόγος“ γέγονε „σὰρξ,“ ὄψεται πῶς ἰδών τις τὴν εἰκόνα „τοῦ ἀοράτου θεοῦ“ γνώσεται „τὸν πατέρα καὶ ποιητὴν τοῦδε τοῦ παντός.“
pass_a_gloss: But also Plato, saying that the one "having found" (εὑρίσκω) it is "impossible" "to say to all" "the maker and father of the all", does not say him to be unspeakable (ἄρρητος) and unnameable (ἀκατονόμαστος), but being speakable (ῥητός) to be able to be spoken to few (ὀλίγοι). Then as if having forgotten (ἐπιλανθάνομαι) the words of Plato he set beside (παρατίθημι), Celsus says God is unnameable in these: "and since for the sake of this it has been found out by wise men, so that we might take some conception of the unnameable and first." But we say not only God to be unspeakable but also others of those after him; which Paul, forcing/straining (βιάζομαι) to signify (σημαίνω), says: "he heard (ἀκούω) unspeakable words (ῥήματα), which it is not permitted (ἔξεστι) for a man to speak (λαλέω)", using "heard" instead of "understood" (συνίημι), analogously to "the one having ears to hear, let him hear". "The maker" then "and father of the all" we say to see (ὁράω, ἰδεῖν) is "a task". And he is seen (βλέπω) not only according to "blessed (μακάριος) the pure (καθαρός) in heart (καρδία), for they will see God", but also according to what is said by the image (εἰκών) "of the invisible (ἀόρατος) God" in "the one having seen me has seen the Father who sent me". For in these no one having sense (νοῦς) would say that Jesus, referring (ἀναφέρω) these to his sensible (αἰσθητός) body (σῶμα) seen by men, said: "the one having seen me ..."; for according to this all who say "crucify, crucify him" will have seen the Father God, and Pilate who received authority (ἐξουσία) over his human [part] (τὸ ἀνθρώπινον), which is absurd (ἄτοπος). That "the one having seen me ..." is not referred to the commoner reception/interpretation (κοινοτέρα ἐκδοχή) is clear from its being said to Philip: "so long a time I am with you, and you have not known (γινώσκω) me, Philip?" And he said this to him asking (ἀξιόω) and saying: "show (δείκνυμι) us the Father, and it suffices (ἀρκέω) us." Having understood (νοέω) then how one must hear (ἀκούω) about the only-begotten (μονογενής) God, Son of God, the firstborn (πρωτότοκος) "of all creation (κτίσις)", inasmuch as "the Word" became "flesh", one will see how one having seen the image "of the invisible God" will know "the father and maker of this all".
pass_b_english: Moreover, when Plato says that “having found” “the maker and father of the universe”, it is “impossible to declare him to all”, he does not say that he is beyond speech and nameless, but that, being expressible, he can be spoken of to a few. Then Celsus, as though he had forgotten the words of Plato that he quoted, says that God is nameless, in these words: “But since, for this reason, wise men have devised a means by which we might grasp some idea of the Nameless and First.”

We, however, say that not only God is beyond speech, but also other things that come after him. Paul, straining to point to these, says: “He heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Corinthians 12:4). He uses “heard” in place of “understood”, as in the saying, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8; Matthew 11:15).

As for “the maker and father of the universe”, we say that to see him is “a hard task”. Yet he is seen, not only in keeping with the words, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), but also in keeping with what is said by the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15): “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” (John 14:9; John 12:45). For no one with any sense would say that in these words Jesus was referring to his body, which could be perceived by the senses and was visible to men, when he said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me.” For on that reading all who said, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:21), would have seen God the Father, and so would Pilate, who received authority over his human nature; and that is absurd.

That the words “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” are not to be taken in the commoner sense is clear from what was said to Philip: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” (John 14:9). He said this to him when he made the request, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). Whoever, then, has understood how we must take what is said about the only-begotten God (John 1:18), the Son of God, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), inasmuch as “the Word” became “flesh” (John 1:14), will see how anyone who has seen the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15) will know “the Father and maker of this universe”.

choices.choice: Origen shifts Plato’s εὑρεῖν (find) to ἰδεῖν (see) in “we say that to see him is a hard task”, deliberately, to lead into the texts on seeing God; kept as “see”. “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” conflates John 14:9 (ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακεν τὸν πατέρα) with John 12:45 (ὁ θεωρῶν ἐμὲ θεωρεῖ τὸν πέμψαντά με); both cited at first occurrence. “He who has ears to hear” also at Mark 4:9 and Luke 8:8; Matthew 11:15 cited as representative. σταύρου σταύρου αὐτόν matches Luke 23:21 exactly (John 19:6 has σταύρωσον). Pilate’s ἐξουσία alludes to John 19:10-11; not cited inline as it is a narrative reference rather than a quotation. μονογενοῦς θεοῦ reflects the reading μονογενὴς θεός at John 1:18; rendered “the only-begotten God”. τὸ ἀνθρώπινον αὐτοῦ: “his human nature” (lit. “his human [part]”). βιασάμενος: “straining” (forcing language to signify what is beyond speech). Review: Origen’s form ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω matches Luke 8:8 exactly (and Luke 14:35); Matthew 11:15 in the critical text lacks ἀκούειν, so Luke 8:8 is now cited first.
